families.source: UKHSA Lyme disease differential diagnosis guidance
families.topic: differentiating erythema migrans, neurological and non-specific symptoms from other conditions
evidence_points: The guidance helps distinguish Lyme disease from other causes of rash, neurological symptoms and non-specific illness.
Erythema migrans commonly appears between 1 and 4 weeks after a tick bite but may appear later.
Erythema migrans can have several appearances and is not always a classic bullseye.
The guidance addresses neurological presentations that may require laboratory investigation.
It considers persistent non-specific systemic symptoms in the differential diagnosis.
It identifies other infections associated with tick bites as alternative explanations.
Clinical history should include tick exposure, geography and symptom timing.
Rash appearance should be considered with evolution over time and other clinical findings.
Absence of a remembered tick bite or classic bullseye rash does not by itself exclude Lyme disease.
Non-specific symptoms alone do not confirm Lyme disease and require appropriate differential diagnosis and testing.

families.source: UKHSA interim Clostridioides difficile prevention and control guidance
families.topic: current interim infection-control, environmental-hygiene and incidence-management guidance for Clostridioides difficile infection
families.page_title: Clostridioides difficile infection: how to deal with the problem
evidence_points: The publication is an interim update to national Clostridioides difficile prevention and control guidance.
It supersedes outdated parts of the earlier 2008 guidance.
It retains relevant principles on infection control and environmental hygiene.
It links users to newer guidance where earlier chapters have been superseded.
It addresses Clostridioides difficile infection in healthcare and community contexts.
It includes updated material on periods of increased incidence.
It distinguishes current interim recommendations from withdrawn historical content.
A full review of management and prevention guidance is still in progress.
Detection or carriage of C. difficile does not by itself establish symptomatic infection.
Response requires symptoms, testing, antibiotic exposure, transmission context and current local infection-control assessment.

families.source: UKHSA Candidozyma auris guidance for acute healthcare settings
families.topic: laboratory investigation, screening, management, IPC, notification and information sharing for C. auris
families.page_title: Candidozyma auris: guidance for acute healthcare settings
evidence_points: Candidozyma auris is an emerging fungal pathogen associated with colonisation, invasive infection and healthcare outbreaks.
The organism can show resistance to multiple antifungal classes.
The guidance covers laboratory investigation in acute healthcare settings.
It provides recommendations for screening patients and contacts.
It addresses management of colonised and infected patients.
It sets out infection prevention and control measures for healthcare environments.
It includes notification, reporting and information-sharing requirements.
The guidance is intended for laboratories, healthcare providers and infection-control teams.
Colonisation does not mean that a patient has an invasive C. auris infection.
Management requires specimen results, symptoms, risk factors, epidemiological links and setting-specific IPC assessment.

families.source: UKHSA Candidozyma auris information for patients and visitors
families.topic: carriage, infection, testing, treatment, hygiene, transfer disclosure and visitor precautions for C. auris
families.page_title: Candidozyma auris: information for patients and visitors
evidence_points: C. auris can be carried on the body without causing symptoms.
Carriage is described as colonisation and is different from infection.
Patients may be screened using swabs from sites such as the armpit, groin and nose.
Antifungal treatment is not normally used to remove asymptomatic carriage.
People with invasive devices or wounds may have a greater risk of infection.
Hospitals may use a single room and additional precautions to reduce spread.
Patients should tell healthcare settings about previous C. auris carriage on later admissions.
Hand hygiene and cleaning measures are important for patients, staff and visitors.
Healthy visitors do not usually become infected, but they can carry the organism transiently.
A positive screening result must be interpreted as carriage or infection using symptoms, specimen site and clinical assessment.

families.source: UKHSA framework of actions to contain carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales
families.topic: screening, recognition, IPC, communication and coordinated containment of CPE in healthcare
evidence_points: The framework focuses on carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales that can spread rapidly in healthcare settings.
CPE creates significant clinical, operational and financial consequences for healthcare providers.
The publication sets out coordinated actions intended to minimise transmission and impact.
Containment depends on early recognition and appropriate screening pathways.
Infection prevention and control measures are central to reducing spread.
Communication during admission, transfer and discharge supports continuity of precautions.
Healthcare organisations should use the framework to develop local policies and response plans.
Implementation should be proportionate to the organism, patient and setting.
Colonisation with CPE is not the same as symptomatic infection.
Response requires microbiology, patient risk factors, contact history, setting and local IPC assessment.
